conceptTag: Groupon restates its revenue before its IPO
readerTitle: Groupon's revenue halved in three months, and nothing changed but the definition
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Groupon, 2011년 IPO 전 매출 정정) + 가상 적용 (쿠폰 1장 계산, 화물 중개업체)
insight: 매출은 내 손을 거쳐 간 돈이 아니라 내가 맡은 역할로 번 돈이다. 거래의 주체(principal)인지 중개자(agent)인지가 매출 크기를 정한다.
misconception: 고객이 나에게 낸 돈은 전부 내 매출이다. 비용으로 빼서 이익만 같으면 매출을 어떻게 잡든 상관없다.

sources.text: Groupon, Inc. Form S-1 registration statement (filed June 2011), SEC EDGAR: 2010년 매출 총액 기준 약 $713.4M
Groupon, Inc. amended Form S-1 (September 2011), SEC EDGAR: 순액 기준으로 정정한 2010년 매출 약 $312.9M
Reuters, The Wall Street Journal 등 2011년 9월 보도: SEC 검토 후 Groupon이 매출 표시 방식을 총액에서 순액으로 변경
Groupon, Inc. Form 8-K and Form 10-K (March 2012): 2011년 4분기 실적 수정, 환불 충당금 부족, 내부통제 중대한 취약점
US GAAP의 principal vs agent (총액 vs 순액) 판단 기준: 당시 EITF 99-19, 현재 ASC 606

factChecks.note: 2010년 매출 $713.4M(최초 S-1, 총액) → $312.9M(수정 S-1, 순액) 수치를 SEC EDGAR 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 차트 값은 백만 달러 단위입니다.
최초 S-1 제출 2011년 6월, 순액 기준 수정 제출 2011년 9월, IPO 2011년 11월 날짜를 확인하세요. 카드에는 월 단위까지만 적었습니다.
총액→순액 정정은 상인 지급액을 매출원가에서 빼고 매출에서도 뺀 것이므로 순손실은 바뀌지 않았다는 서술을 수정 S-1로 확인하세요.
2012년 3월 4분기 실적 수정(환불 충당금 부족)과 감사인의 내부통제 중대한 취약점(material weakness) 지적을 Groupon 10-K로 확인하세요.
쿠폰 예시는 가상 수치: 고객 지불 $50, 상인 몫 $25, Groupon 몫 $25 (실제 배분 비율은 거래마다 달랐음). 화물 예시: $2,000 − $1,700 = $300.
화물 중개업체는 계약 조건에 따라 총액(주체) 또는 순액(중개자)으로 보고할 수 있습니다. 실제로 일부 대형 중개업체는 총액으로 보고합니다. 그래서 적용 문제의 정답을 '조건에 따라 다르다'로 두었습니다. 특정 국가의 회계 조언이 아닙니다.

cards.title: Groupon's revenue halved in three months, and nothing changed but the definition
body: In June 2011, Groupon filed to go public. Its papers showed 2010 revenue of about **$713 million**.
A few months later, the same year's revenue read about $313 million. No deals were cancelled. No customers asked for refunds. Only one question had been answered differently: whose money was it?

image.label: One pile of money shrinking by half under a magnifying glass
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 책상 위 동전 더미에 돋보기를 대니 절반은 식당 앞치마를 두른 손으로 넘어가고 절반만 남는 장면. 실제 Groupon 로고나 색상은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A customer pays you $50 for a meal voucher.
body: You run a daily-deals site. A customer pays you $50 for a $100 voucher at a local restaurant. You keep $25 and pass $25 to the restaurant, which cooks and serves the meal.
What should you report as revenue?

options.text: $50, the full amount the customer paid you
options.feedback: The cash did come to you, but half was never yours to keep. This makes your business look twice as big as it is.

options.text: $25, your share for arranging the deal
options.feedback: You didn't cook the meal. You earned a fee for bringing the customer. Your revenue is that fee, even though more cash passed through your account.

options.text: $50, with the restaurant's $25 listed as a cost, so profit stays the same
options.feedback: Profit is indeed the same. But revenue is what people use to judge your size and growth, so it still overstates the business.

choice.afterReveal: Option C is close to what Groupon first did.

cards.title: Same year, same deals, two revenue numbers.
body: Groupon first counted the full price of each voucher as revenue and the merchant's share as a cost. After review by US securities regulators, it refiled in September 2011 counting only its own share.
Its losses didn't change. Its reported revenue fell by more than half. Groupon went public that November.

cards.title: Principal or agent: gross vs net revenue
body: If you are the **principal**, you own the promise to the customer. You control the product or service and carry the risk if it goes wrong. You report the full price as revenue: *gross*.
If you are the **agent**, you arrange for someone else to deliver. You report only your fee: *net*.
The restaurant cooked the meal and owned the dining experience. Groupon brought the diner in. That made it an agent.

image.label: Two paths: seller who delivers vs middleman who connects
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Principal": 가게 주인이 직접 상품을 건네고 "Full price = revenue". 오른쪽 "Agent": 중개인이 손님과 가게를 연결하고 작은 동전만 받음 "Your fee = revenue". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Profit stayed put. The story didn't.
body: If profit is the same either way, why fight over the label? Because readers use revenue as a ruler.
Investors compare a company's price to its revenue. Halve the revenue and the company looks twice as expensive. Growth rates, market share and margins all lean on the top line.
A gross number made Groupon look like a giant retailer. A net number showed a marketing business earning fees.

cards.title: Anyone who sits in the middle faces this choice.
body: Travel agents, ticket sellers, wholesalers who drop-ship, staffing agencies and freight brokers all handle money that partly belongs to someone else.
The test is not who collects the cash. It's who makes the promise, sets the price and absorbs the loss when something fails.
cards.softwareNote: App stores, ride-hailing apps and online marketplaces face the same question. A platform that just connects buyers and sellers usually reports its commission, while one that sells its own inventory reports the full price.

cards.title: Net isn't always right, and one fix isn't the end.
body: Some middlemen really are principals. If you set the price, guarantee delivery and eat the loss when a supplier fails, gross may be correct. The rules call for judgment, not a default.

And a corrected label doesn't make every number reliable. In early 2012, months after its IPO, Groupon revised its late-2011 results after setting aside too little for refunds, and its auditor flagged weak internal controls.

cards.title: Now it's a freight broker.
body: You own no trucks. A manufacturer pays you $2,000 to move a load. You hire a carrier for $1,700 and keep $300.
What's your revenue on this job?

options.feedback: Sending the invoice doesn't settle it. Groupon collected the cash too, and that alone didn't make the full amount its revenue.

options.text: $300, because you don't own the trucks
options.feedback: Often right, but owning trucks isn't the test. A broker can be the principal without owning a single vehicle.

options.text: It depends on whether you promised the delivery, set the price and carry the loss if it fails
options.feedback: If you're on the hook to the shipper, $2,000 may be right. If you just connect shipper and carrier for a fee, report $300.

cards.title: Revenue is what you earn for your role, not the money that passes through.
body: Before you report a sale, ask whose promise the customer is buying.
**Try it today:** list each way your business brings in money. For each, ask: if this goes wrong, who does the customer blame, and who pays to fix it?
